text: Transitions for every character; matrix power.

The KMP automaton (KMP 自动机) turns a pattern of length m into states 0 … m ("how many characters of the pattern currently match") with a transition for every character: go[j][c] = j + 1 if p[j+1] = c, else go[nxt[j]][c] (with go[0][c] = 0 on a mismatch). It is the one-pattern case of the AC automaton (拓展篇第2章).

Counting strings of length n that avoid the pattern: DP over (length, state), never entering state m. When n is huge (GT 考试 P3193: n up to 10⁹), the transition is the same every step, so build the (m × m) transition matrix and raise it to the n-th power (进阶篇第22章): O(m³ log n).
Digit strings of length n that do not contain the pattern, modulo K; checked by listing all 10ⁿ strings in Python for small n. The matrix entry T[j][k] counts digits that move state j to state k.
Duval's three pointers; minimal rotation.

A Lyndon word is strictly smaller than all of its proper suffixes (equivalently, than all its rotations), e.g. "aab", "abb". Every string splits uniquely into Lyndon words w1 ≥ w2 ≥ … ≥ wk (Chen–Fox–Lyndon).
Duval's algorithm finds this factorisation in O(n) with three pointers.

Duval: i = start of the current block, j = compare position, k = scan position. While s[k] ≥ s[j]: if equal, advance both (a repeat of a Lyndon word is forming); if larger, j = i (the whole prefix becomes one longer Lyndon word). When s[k] < s[j], output copies of length k − j and restart after them. The minimal rotation of a string starts at the last Lyndon factor of s + s that begins in the first half (P1368 工艺).

Prints the end position of every factor (P6114 combines these into one XOR). Checked against the definition in Python: repeatedly take the longest prefix that is a Lyndon word.
Order-free child hashes; centroid roots.

Tree hashing (树哈希) decides whether two trees are isomorphic. For a rooted tree, compute each vertex's hash from the multiset of its children's hashes, in a way that does not depend on their order, e.g. h(u) = 1 + Σ f(h(child)) with a fixed scrambling function f (xor-shift on 64-bit), or by sorting the children's hashes.

For unrooted trees, root at the centroid (there are one or two): two trees are isomorphic iff their hashes rooted at their centroids match (taking the smaller of two). A plain sum of child hashes collides easily; the scrambling function f is what makes it reliable (树同构 P5043).

Ukkonen's algorithm builds a suffix tree online in O(n) using an "active point" and suffix links between internal nodes. It is long and fragile; in contests use the suffix automaton of the reversed string (whose link tree is the suffix tree, 拓展篇第33章) or a suffix array instead.

title: 序列自动机与二维哈希

text: nxt[i][c]; row hash then column hash.

The subsequence automaton (序列自动机): nxt[i][c] = the first position j > i with sj = c (0 if none), filled from the back in O(n · Σ). Testing whether t is a subsequence of s is then one jump per character, O(|t|); it greedily takes the earliest match, which is always safe.

The automaton is a DAG whose paths from state 0 are exactly the distinct subsequences, so DP on it counts them: f(i) = 1 + Σc f(nxt[i][c]), answer f(0) − 1 for nonempty ones. Common subsequences of two strings = paths in both automata at once (P5826 is the template).

Subsequence tests and the count of distinct nonempty subsequences, checked in Python by listing all 2¹² subsequences of s.

2D hashing (二维哈希): hash each row's windows of width b with base P (unsigned overflow as mod 2⁶⁴), then hash each column of those row hashes over windows of height a with a second base Q. A matrix window then has one number, compared to the pattern's in O(1): counting occurrences of an a × b pattern in an n × m text is O(nm).

Same rules as 1D hashing (拓展篇): two different bases for the two directions, and use two moduli or random bases if the problem is adversarial. Prefix-sum style 2D hashes H(i, j) also allow any submatrix in O(1): H = h(x2, y2) − h(x1, y2)·Qa − h(x2, y1)·Pb + h(x1, y1)·PbQa.

Key points to memorise
1. KMP automaton: go[j][c] = j+1 on match, else go[nxt[j]][c]; avoid state m.
2. Fixed transitions over many steps ⇒ matrix power.
3. Lyndon: smaller than all proper suffixes; unique factorisation w1 ≥ w2 ≥ ….
4. Duval: s[k] > s[j] ⇒ j = i; equal ⇒ j++; smaller ⇒ output periods of length k − j.
5. Tree hash: h(u) = 1 + Σ mix(h(child)); unrooted ⇒ root at centroid(s).
6. Subsequence automaton: nxt[i][c] from the back; paths = distinct subsequences.
7. 2D hash: base P along rows, base Q down columns.
